title: Pathophysiology: Cardiovascular Hemodynamics—Cardiac Output, Ischemia and Heart Failure
html:
Cardiovascular pathophysiology asks whether the heart can fill, eject, and deliver enough oxygenated blood to meet tissue needs without creating harmful filling pressures. A blood pressure, heart rate, ejection fraction, or edema finding is only one part of that question. The RN connects hemodynamics with symptoms, examination findings, rhythm, oxygenation, kidney and neurologic function, laboratory trends, and response to treatment.

Learning goals

  • Relate heart rate and stroke volume to cardiac output.
  • Explain how preload, afterload, contractility, and ventricular compliance affect stroke volume.
  • Distinguish pressure, flow, congestion, and tissue perfusion.
  • Connect coronary perfusion and myocardial oxygen supply–demand balance to ischemia.
  • Compare systolic and diastolic dysfunction without relying on ejection fraction alone.
  • Recognize left- and right-sided congestion and low-output findings.
  • Explain short-term compensation and long-term maladaptive remodeling.
  • Prioritize acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary edema, dysrhythmia, and cardiogenic shock cues.

Cardiac output links the pump to perfusion

Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Stroke volume is the amount ejected with each beat and equals end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. Cardiac index adjusts output for body surface area, but neither value alone describes whether every organ is adequately perfused.

A faster heart rate can raise output initially, but excessive tachycardia shortens diastolic filling and coronary perfusion time while increasing myocardial oxygen demand. Bradycardia may reduce output when stroke volume cannot compensate. Rhythm matters: loss of coordinated atrial or ventricular contraction can reduce filling and forward flow even when the displayed rate appears acceptable.

Preload, afterload, contractility, and compliance shape stroke volume

Preload reflects ventricular stretch at the end of filling and is influenced by venous return, circulating volume, chamber compliance, and filling time. Within physiologic limits, greater filling can increase contraction through the Frank–Starling relationship. Beyond the useful range—or when the ventricle is weak or stiff—more filling pressure may mainly worsen pulmonary or systemic congestion.

Afterload is the load the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Arterial pressure and vascular resistance contribute, but afterload is not identical to one blood-pressure value. Greater afterload tends to reduce stroke volume and increase the amount of blood left after systole. Chronic hypertension or outflow obstruction can produce hypertrophy and eventually impair filling or ejection.

Contractility is the myocardium's intrinsic ability to generate force at a given preload and afterload. Ischemia, infarction, acidosis, severe hypoxemia, inflammatory injury, and selected medications can reduce it. Sympathetic stimulation can increase rate and contractility temporarily, but at the cost of higher oxygen demand.

Compliance describes how readily a chamber expands during filling. A stiff ventricle may have a preserved ejection fraction yet require high filling pressure to receive a smaller end-diastolic volume. This is why preserved ejection fraction does not exclude heart failure.

Pressure is not the same as flow
Mean arterial pressure is influenced by cardiac output and vascular resistance. Vasoconstriction may preserve a seemingly acceptable pressure while cardiac output and tissue perfusion fall. Assess mentation, urine output, skin temperature, capillary refill, pulses, lactate trend, and organ function with the blood pressure.

Coronary perfusion must match myocardial demand

The myocardium extracts a large proportion of delivered oxygen at rest, so rising demand is met mainly by increasing coronary blood flow. Supply depends on coronary patency and tone, perfusion pressure, diastolic time, arterial oxygen content, and collateral flow. Demand rises with tachycardia, contractility, wall tension, and afterload.

Ischemia occurs when oxygen supply cannot meet demand. Atherosclerotic plaque and thrombosis are important causes, but hypotension, hypoxemia, severe anemia, tachyarrhythmia, or markedly increased afterload can also create a mismatch. Ischemia may be reversible; prolonged severe ischemia can cause myocardial necrosis and loss of contractile tissue.

Chest pressure, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, unusual fatigue, syncope, or acute hemodynamic change can be ischemic presentations. Absence of classic chest pain does not rule out acute coronary syndrome. New symptoms require timely assessment, ECG acquisition according to protocol, escalation, and prescribed evaluation rather than waiting for a single biomarker.

Heart failure can reflect impaired ejection, filling, or both

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which structural or functional cardiac impairment produces symptoms and signs from inadequate output, elevated filling pressures, or both. In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, impaired systolic contraction commonly lowers stroke volume and raises end-systolic and filling volumes. In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, impaired relaxation and increased stiffness can raise filling pressure despite a preserved fraction ejected.

Ejection fraction is the stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume. It describes a proportion, not the absolute amount of blood delivered to tissues. A client can have a preserved fraction of a small end-diastolic volume, or a reduced fraction with temporarily adequate perfusion. Diagnosis and severity require the entire clinical picture.

Congestion and hypoperfusion create different cue clusters

Left-sided congestion raises pressure behind the left ventricle and can produce exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, hypoxemia, cough, and pulmonary edema. Right-sided congestion can produce jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, ascites, hepatic congestion, and weight gain. Either side can affect the other, and biventricular findings are common.

Low forward output may produce fatigue, cool or mottled skin, weak pulses, delayed capillary refill, oliguria, altered mentation, dizziness, rising lactate, and worsening kidney or liver function. Congestion and hypoperfusion can coexist. Daily weight and intake/output trends help assess fluid balance, but a rapid clinical decline outranks routine measurements.

Compensation protects first and harms later

When output falls, sympathetic activation raises heart rate, contractility, and vascular tone. The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and vasopressin promote vasoconstriction and sodium and water retention. These responses may support pressure and perfusion in the short term.

Persistent activation increases afterload, filling pressure, oxygen demand, edema, and ventricular wall stress. Hypertrophy, dilation, fibrosis, and altered chamber geometry—collectively called remodeling—can further impair function. Natriuretic peptides oppose some sodium retention and vasoconstriction, but their laboratory values are influenced by age, kidney function, body composition, rhythm, and timing; they support rather than independently establish a diagnosis.

Valve disease creates pressure or volume overload

Stenosis obstructs forward flow and creates pressure overload upstream. Regurgitation allows backward flow and creates volume overload. The consequences depend on the valve, severity, acuity, heart rate, ventricular adaptation, and pulmonary pressures. Chronic disease may be compensated for years; acute severe regurgitation can produce abrupt pulmonary edema or shock before chamber enlargement develops.

A murmur describes turbulent flow, not the full severity of the lesion. New dyspnea, chest discomfort, syncope, hypotension, pulmonary edema, or reduced perfusion in a client with suspected valve disease requires urgent evaluation.

Dysrhythmias affect both rate and coordinated filling

Tachyarrhythmias can shorten filling time, raise oxygen demand, and reduce stroke volume. Bradyarrhythmias can lower cardiac output. Loss of atrial contraction may be poorly tolerated by a stiff ventricle, while uncoordinated ventricular activity can eliminate effective output entirely.

Treat the client, not only the monitor. Assess pulse, blood pressure, mentation, chest symptoms, breathing, oxygenation, and perfusion; verify lead connection and obtain a diagnostic tracing when indicated. Hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic discomfort, acute heart failure, or signs of shock signal instability and require immediate escalation according to emergency protocols.

Cardiogenic shock is pump failure with organ hypoperfusion

Cardiogenic shock can follow extensive infarction, severe ventricular failure, mechanical complications, acute valve failure, myocarditis, or serious dysrhythmia. Falling output triggers vasoconstriction that may temporarily support pressure but increases afterload and myocardial workload. Coronary perfusion can fall, worsening ischemia and contractility in a self-reinforcing cycle.

Possible cues include hypotension or narrowing pulse pressure, cool clammy skin, weak pulses, altered mentation, oliguria, rising lactate, pulmonary congestion, neck-vein distention, dysrhythmia, and chest symptoms. Not every client displays every finding, and early shock may precede profound hypotension.

Escalate the pattern, not just a number
New chest pressure with diaphoresis, acute pulmonary edema, worsening work of breathing, symptomatic dysrhythmia, syncope, new confusion, cool mottled skin, or falling urine output can signal cardiovascular instability even before a dramatic blood-pressure change.

Hemodynamic interventions can help one variable and harm another

Fluids may improve stroke volume when inadequate preload is limiting output, but can worsen congestion when filling pressure is already high. Vasodilators may reduce afterload or preload but can cause hypotension. Vasopressors may support perfusion pressure while increasing afterload or ischemic risk. Inotropes may improve contractility while increasing dysrhythmia and oxygen-demand risk. Diuresis may relieve congestion but requires monitoring of pressure, kidney function, and electrolytes.

The RN verifies indication, access, dose, compatibility, monitoring parameters, and titration authority; evaluates the client before and after intervention; and communicates trends promptly. A favorable blood-pressure change is incomplete evidence if mentation, urine output, breathing, perfusion, or organ function worsens.

Translate cardiovascular physiology into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify symptoms, onset, rhythm, heart rate, blood-pressure trend, pulse pressure, oxygenation, lung and heart sounds, neck veins, edema, pulses, skin, mentation, urine output, weight, ECG, laboratory data, and therapies.
  2. Analyze cues: Organize findings as impaired filling, excessive afterload, reduced contractility, dysrhythmia, ischemia, congestion, low forward flow, or a mixed pattern.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary edema, unstable dysrhythmia, mechanical complication, and cardiogenic shock outrank chronic stable findings.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan ABC support, monitoring, ECG and laboratory evaluation, prescribed hemodynamic therapy, fluid strategy, electrolyte safeguards, and escalation.
  5. Take action: Position and support the client, activate the appropriate response, implement time-sensitive orders and protocols, and communicate the complete trend.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, work of breathing, oxygenation, rhythm, pressure, pulses, skin, mentation, urine output, congestion, laboratory trends, and treatment harms.

Clinical example

A client with an acute myocardial infarction becomes restless and cool. Blood pressure is lower than baseline, heart rate is 118/min, urine output is declining, crackles are increasing, and lactate is rising. The RN recognizes a cluster of impaired contractility, pulmonary congestion, and systemic hypoperfusion—not simply anxiety or one abnormal number. The RN activates urgent escalation, supports airway and oxygenation as indicated, obtains continuous rhythm and hemodynamic monitoring, implements prescribed therapy, and evaluates perfusion and congestion repeatedly.
